newsitem.title: UGANDA: Prices soar in Uganda capital as traders strike.
newsitem.headline: Prices soar in Uganda capital as traders strike.

text.p: Consumer prices rose in the Ugandan capital Kampala on Thursday as a traders' strike against a new government tax entered its fourth day.

Officials said the strike, which started on Monday in protest against a new 17 percent Value Added Tax (VAT) on all processed goods, had also spread to towns and cities outside Kampala. The new tax took effect on July 1 this year.

Shops in Kampala's central business section remained closed and police patrolled the deserted streets. Only markets selling food items were opened and the striking traders threatened to loot shops defying their order to close.
The traders are demanding that the government scrap the tax and return instead to the 15 percent Commercial Transaction Levy (CTL) which VAT replaced.

Finance minister Jehoash Mayanja-Nkangi has said he will not review the tax, saying the cash-strapped state would lose up to one billion shillings ($910,000) for each percentage point reduction in the tax.
President Yoweri Museveni held a crisis meeting with his cabinet on Wednesday and Thursday to try and find a way to end the strike, which has paralysed business.

Shoppers in Kampala suburbs said prices for sugar, milk, eggs, agricultural produce and a range of other consumer goods rose by between 20 and 50 percent as traders defied a government directive to reopen their shops.
Private radio stations and reporters reached by telephone said the strike had affected all the key towns upcountry, and only offices, banks and food markets were open for business.
More policemen were deployed on the streets of the capital after traders threatened to force fuel stations to close.

The traders have complained they were misled by a one-year- long education campaign ahead of the introduction of the tax. President Museveni said during his campaign for a May election, which he won decisively, that the tax would affect only about 7,000 of the biggest traders.

Consumer prices rose immediately the tax came into effect, but most traders started feeling the effects only after the state Uganda Revenue Authority (URA) tightened its noose on defaulting businessmen.
URA commissioner-general, Ghanaian Larbi Siaw declined to talk to reporters about the possible fate of the tax, saying he was awaiting a decision from the cabinet meeting on Thursday.
Ghana abolished VAT after riots swept the capital Accra.
Finance ministry officials declined to comment on the strike, which they said had cost them some 10 billion shillings in potential revenue since it started.
Economic analysts said the strike posed a major challenge to plans by the reformist president to reduce Uganda's dependence on foreign aid.
